title: Introduction to Coordinate Geometry
content: Have you ever tried to find your seat in a movie theater? You first look for the row (like Row G) and then your seat number (like Seat 12). Coordinate geometry is a mathematical version of this exact process. It helps us locate the exact position of a point in a plane.

title: René Descartes and the Ceiling Fly
content: The system we use was developed by the French mathematician René Descartes in the 17th century. Legend has it that he was lying in bed, watching a fly crawl on the ceiling, and realized he could describe its exact position by measuring its distance from two adjacent walls.

title: Cartesian System
content: The Cartesian coordinate system is a coordinate system that specifies each point uniquely in a plane by a set of numerical coordinates, which are the signed distances to the point from two fixed perpendicular oriented lines, measured in the same unit of length.

title: The Number Lines: X and Y Axes
content: The Cartesian plane is formed by two mutually perpendicular number lines. The horizontal line is called the **x-axis** (often denoted as X'OX). The vertical line is called the **y-axis** (often denoted as Y'OY). These two axes together are known as the **coordinate axes**.

title: Origin
content: The point where the x-axis and the y-axis intersect is called the **Origin**. It is denoted by the letter 'O' and serves as the starting reference point for all measurements in the Cartesian plane.

title: Coordinates of Origin
content: The coordinates of the origin are always O(0, 0).

title: Quadrants
content: The two coordinate axes divide the Cartesian plane into four equal parts. Each of these parts is called a **Quadrant**. They are numbered I, II, III, and IV in an anti-clockwise direction, starting from the positive x-axis and positive y-axis.

title: Signs in Quadrants
content:
Quadrant I: (+, +)
Quadrant II: (-, +)
Quadrant III: (-, -)
Quadrant IV: (+, -)

title: Abscissa and Ordinate
content: Every point in the Cartesian plane has two coordinates. The x-coordinate represents the perpendicular distance from the y-axis and is called the **Abscissa**. The y-coordinate represents the perpendicular distance from the x-axis and is called the **Ordinate**.

title: Walk Before You Jump
content: When plotting a point (x, y), always think: 'Walk along the ground (x-axis) first, then climb the ladder (y-axis).' This helps prevent mixing up the x and y coordinates.

title: Swapping Coordinates
content: One of the most common mistakes in coordinate geometry is swapping the x and y values. The point (3, 5) is completely different from the point (5, 3). In (3, 5), you move 3 units on the x-axis and 5 units on the y-axis. In (5, 3), you move 5 units on the x-axis and 3 units on the y-axis.

title: Plotting a Point P(3, 4)
content:
Step 1: Start at the origin (0,0).
Step 2: Move 3 units to the right along the positive x-axis.
Step 3: From there, move 4 units upwards, parallel to the positive y-axis.
Step 4: Mark the point and label it P(3, 4).

title: Plotting a Point with Negative Coordinates Q(-2, -5)
content:
Step 1: Start at the origin (0,0).
Step 2: Move 2 units to the left along the negative x-axis.
Step 3: From there, move 5 units downwards, parallel to the negative y-axis.
Step 4: Mark the point and label it Q(-2, -5). Notice that both coordinates are negative, which places it in Quadrant III.

title: Points on the Axes
content: What happens if a point lies directly on one of the axes? If a point lies on the x-axis, its vertical distance from the x-axis is zero, so its y-coordinate is 0. Its form is (x, 0). Conversely, if a point lies on the y-axis, its horizontal distance from the y-axis is zero, so its x-coordinate is 0. Its form is (0, y).

title: Points on the Y-Axis
content: Students often incorrectly plot (0, 4) on the x-axis instead of the y-axis. Remember, if x = 0, you do not move left or right at all. You stay on the y-axis and move 4 units up.

title: Finding Distance from Axes
content:
Given a point R(6, -2), find its perpendicular distance from the x-axis and the y-axis.
Solution:
The perpendicular distance from the x-axis is the absolute value of the y-coordinate = |-2| = 2 units.
The perpendicular distance from the y-axis is the absolute value of the x-coordinate = |6| = 6 units.

title: Distance from Axes Formula
content:
For any point P(x, y):
Distance from x-axis = |y|
Distance from y-axis = |x|

title: Identify the Coordinates
content: Look at a standard Cartesian plane. If you start at the origin, move 4 units left, and 7 units up, what are the coordinates of your final position? What quadrant are you in?

title: Chapter Summary
content:
- The Cartesian plane is formed by two intersecting perpendicular lines called axes.
- The horizontal line is the x-axis, the vertical line is the y-axis.
- The point of intersection is the Origin (0,0).
- The axes divide the plane into 4 Quadrants.
- Any point is defined by (x, y) where x is the abscissa and y is the ordinate.
- Points on the x-axis are (x, 0) and points on the y-axis are (0, y).
